passage: The evening news showed crowds outside the collectorate, and Neelam switched it off. “I'm not thinking about any of this,” she told her brother Raghav, who was reading about the student council election. “Politics means trouble.” At school, the civics teacher asked for volunteers to debate the flooded drain outside the gate, and Neelam kept her eyes on her desk. When her friends planned an email to the ward councillor, she said she had a headache and left early. Weeks later the drain still overflowed every rainy morning. A friend said, “You write so well, Neelam. You could have helped us.” She had no answer. She didn't know how a petition worked, or what a lawful march looked like, because she had made sure never to learn.

qa.q: What did Neelam do when the news showed crowds?
What was Neelam afraid of when she avoided the debate and the email?
qa.a: Getting into trouble; she said politics means trouble, and staying away felt like the way to avoid the risk.

qa.q: What could Neelam try instead, and why?
qa.a: She could take one small lawful step, such as helping a teacher draft the email to the councillor, since it teaches how public life works while keeping the risk low.

qa.q: How might Raghav see Neelam's decision?
qa.a: Raghav, who cares about the student council election, may see her as capable but closing a door before learning what safe taking part looks like.

grounding: A teen avoids all civic thinking out of fear, staying safe but losing the chance to learn lawful participation.

"Pema, are you coming to the school council meeting on the bus route?" Hrithik asked at the gate.

"No."

"But you're on that bus. It's your route they're cutting."

"I don't do all that," Pema said. "Protests, meetings, petitions. You get into trouble. My uncle got into trouble once. So I just don't think about it."

"Nobody's protesting. It's a council meeting. In the library."

"Same thing."

Two weeks later, Hrithik read out the new timetable in class. The 7:10 bus was gone. The council had agreed to a smaller route after hearing only from students on the other side of town.

Pema's face fell. "They didn't even ask us."

"They did," Hrithik said. "Nobody from our side came."

Pema was quiet all through maths.

qa.q: Where was the council meeting held?
How did Pema feel when the new timetable was read out?
qa.a: Pema felt dismayed and let down, her face falling at losing the 7:10 bus.

qa.q: What approach could Pema have taken instead of avoiding the meeting completely?
qa.a: Pema could have gone to the library meeting and simply explained the bus problem, which is safe and lawful and would have put that side's needs on record.

qa.q: How might Hrithik see Pema's avoidance?
qa.a: Hrithik probably feels frustrated but sympathetic, knowing the fear comes from an uncle's trouble but seeing it cost them the bus.

grounding: Shows a teen avoiding any civic decision out of fear, which avoids risk but removes a chance to take part safely and costs something real.

passage:
Last year, when there were meetings at my school about the new canteen rules, I stayed away from all of it. I'm Jeevan, and in our house we don't "get involved". My grandfather lost a job long ago after speaking at a union meeting, and that story hangs over every conversation.

So I decided: I won't think about any of this. Not the canteen, not the petitions, not the students' council. Safer.

My friend Nikita went to every meeting. She spoke about veg and non-veg counters being separate. She helped write a proposal that the principal accepted.

At the end of the year, the civics teacher asked us to describe one way we'd taken part in school decisions. Nikita wrote two pages. I had nothing.

It wasn't that I'd been in danger. It's that I never learned how to take part safely at all. This year I'm going to one council meeting. Just to listen.

qa.q: What did Nikita speak about at the meetings?
qa.a: About veg and non-veg counters being separate.

qa.q: How did Jeevan feel when there was nothing to write for the civics teacher?
qa.a: Jeevan felt empty-handed and a little ashamed, realising the avoidance had meant missing out on learning.

qa.q: What small step is Jeevan planning, and why is it a good start?
qa.a: Going to one council meeting just to listen; it is low-risk and lawful and lets Jeevan learn how taking part works.

qa.q: How might Nikita see Jeevan's decision to attend one meeting?
qa.a: Nikita would probably feel pleased and welcoming, glad that a friend who stayed away is ready to try.

grounding: A reflective account of a teen who avoided civic issues out of fear, avoiding risk but losing the chance to learn to take part in safe, lawful ways.
